parts.spoken_English: In 1936 the colossal Hindenburg made 17 Atlantic round trips, a marvel of luxury and glamour.
Its amenities included a lounge and, that year, a grand piano.
An American embargo on helium export had left the ship relying on hydrogen.
Because that gas was combustible, smokers sat behind an airlock with one electric lighter.
The airship left Frankfurt on 3 May 1937.
Hours behind its timetable, it met thunderstorms at Lakehurst and circled for over an hour before its descent towards the mooring mast.
At about 7:25 pm on 6 May, flames appeared near the stern.
The inferno incinerated the ship in about half a minute, leaving a crumpled frame.
Of the 97 aboard, 62 survived, a proportion close to two-thirds, while a minority of 35 died, as did one man on the ground.
A 14-year-old cabin boy was drenched by a deluge from a burst water tank, and the soaking saved him.
He dropped through a hatch and scrambled clear, escaping only narrowly.
Newsreel cameras and photographers caught the disaster.
A radio correspondent's eyewitness commentary was not live; audiences heard it the next day.
The cause has not been definitively established, but static electricity igniting leaking hydrogen is the leading explanation.
A theory blaming the doped fabric has been rejected.
The 1933 crash of USS Akron killed 73 yet won less notoriety.
The filmed fire left a fateful image that abruptly wrecked confidence.
As public perception soured, Graf Zeppelin was withdrawn, later scrapped, and a glamorous epoch of aviation closed.
The doomed airship's first journey to North America had begun on 6 May 1936, exactly a year before the fire.
